title: Heritage as curriculum: Intangible cultural heritage examined through a comparative study of visual art education across Japan, Australia and Finland
abstract: Abstract UNESCO mandates have spurred global interest in Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) as a response to global tensions and as a tool for peacebuilding, identity, reconciliation and resilience. The question arises as to how these living traditions might survive the transition into formal education curricula, especially Visual Art Education (VAE), which remains under‐theorised. This article moves beyond viewing heritage as mere ‘content’ to be added to a syllabus, framing the curriculum instead as a site of negotiation where knowledge must be systematically endorsed and stabilised. A comparative analysis of peer‐reviewed articles and national curriculum policies from Japan, Australia and Finland (2015–2025) was carried out using Actor‐Network Theory (ANT) as an analytical lens. The findings disrupt the idea of a universal model for VAE curriculum and point to the inscription‐practice gap. In Japan, the network is characterised by systemic nationalisation, where curricular frameworks and standardised material function as the primary agents for stabilising traditional culture. title: When national qualifications travel: Curriculum fairness after the 2024 Pearson Edexcel A‐Level Chinese reform
abstract: Abstract National qualifications do not always stay national. Once offered internationally, a reform designed around one education system may reach students with very different linguistic histories. This article examines that problem through Pearson Edexcel A‐Level Chinese, an England‐regulated subject qualification offered in the UK and internationally. From 2026, candidates will read the listening and reading questions in English and answer them in English. The change responds to evidence that earlier papers disadvantaged students learning Chinese as an additional language. It also changes how every candidate must show Chinese comprehension to receive credit. The study draws on entry statistics, policy and specification documents, and Pearson's sample paper. Ofqual reported approximately 5150 Pearson entries in 2023, while the Joint Council for Qualifications (JCQ) recorded 1449 UK Chinese A‐Level entries across all awarding organisations. The difference gives a conservative estimate of at least 3701 Pearson entries outside the UK, or 71.9% of Pearson's total. title: Marrying task‐based language teaching and translanguaging: A curriculum‐level case study of a Chinese Tier‐3 vocational university
abstract: Abstract This qualitative case study examines the pedagogically sequenced, complementary deployment of task‐based language teaching (TBLT) and translanguaging within the ESP curriculum of a Chinese Tier‐3 vocational university. Rather than proposing a fully fused theoretical model, the study reframes translanguaging not as an alternative to TBLT but as a phase‐bound mediational resource embedded within a restructured three‐phase task cycle at ECVTU. Distinguished from ad hoc code‐switching, translanguaging functioned as conceptual scaffolding during pre‐task planning, covert affective regulation during performance, and metalinguistic reflection during debriefing. Drawing on 48 h of classroom recordings, stimulated‐recall interviews, and student artefacts, the findings suggest that strategically bounded translanguaging can enhance self‐efficacy and L2 complexity without displacing TBLT's core psycholinguistic demands, while accountability tools mitigated emergent ‘comfort traps’. By drawing on recent research, the study outlines a provisional Synergistic Task Cycle Template aligned with Tylerian sequencing and vocational workplace realities. title: ‘What is the project?’: A fine‐grained study of some key challenges to interdisciplinary teaching and learning in the humanities
abstract: Abstract Interdisciplinary teaching and learning in the humanities (Humanities ITL) has gained prominence in recent decades. Yet to date, empirical research has largely emphasised its benefits and affordances, with far fewer studies examining the challenges it poses. The present study advances our understanding of how such challenges emerge in practice and how they intersect. Drawing on linguistic‐ethnographic methods, a fine‐grained lens is applied to the enactment of Humanities ITL curricular units in two secondary schools. The analysis reveals that the epistemic challenge is distinct from institutional hurdles and more resilient than them, persisting even where institutional support was abundant. Overall, the findings suggest that without deep disciplinary fluency, Humanities ITL risks drifting into parallel disciplinary tracks rather than achieving genuine integration.

title: Using well‐being literacy to align capability‐based learning with well‐being curriculums in Australian secondary schools
abstract: Abstract This reflective piece draws a link between recent work in Well‐being Science and capability‐based learning to increase the transferability of well‐being curriculums. We propose that a capability‐based approach to well‐being curriculum may assist students to activate the skills they need when necessary and may update well‐being curriculums for more impactful learning and engagement.

title: Turkish science curriculum reloaded: Epistemic practice demands in the newly released curricular documents
abstract: Abstract This study investigated the integration of epistemic practices in the 2024 Turkish science curriculums for grades 3–8, addressing the global shift towards a science‐as‐practice (epistemic turn) approach that positions students as epistemic agents engaged in practices like data analysis, argumentation and reasoning. Using a novel, epistemically oriented taxonomy, the study analysed 745 learning outcomes to assess the distribution and alignment of epistemic practice demands with students' cognitive and epistemic development. Findings revealed that while the curriculums incorporate 40 distinct epistemic practices (e.g. data gathering, model construction, inductive reasoning, classifying, control‐of‐variables, evidence‐based reasoning, identifying logical fallacies, experimenting, interrogating), their distribution was inconsistent and misaligned with students' developmental stages. Lower‐order practices (e.g. perception and conception) dominated, while higher‐order practices (e.g. causation, argumentation and abstraction) were underrepresented, potentially hindering students' progression towards advanced epistemic cognition. title: Sustainable governance for improved educational management, administration and leadership: A book review of handbook of best practices in sustainable development at university level. By WalterLeal Filho, Claudio RuyPortela de Vasconcelos (Ed.), Springer Nature. (2022). 498 pages. ISBN: 978‐3‐031‐04763‐3. https://doi.org/10.1007/978‐3‐031‐04764‐0.
Perceptions about Ethnozootechny in Animal Science education in Brazil
abstract: Abstract This study analysed the knowledge and perceptions of students, professors and coordinators regarding Ethnozootechny in Animal Science education in Brazil. A quantitative, descriptive‐exploratory study was conducted using a structured questionnaire applied to 316 participants from Animal Science courses across all five regions of the country. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, inferential tests (Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney) and hierarchical cluster analysis (Ward's method), complemented by principal component analysis. Two distinct groups were identified, representing 87% and 13% of the sample, respectively. More than 70% of respondents in both groups reported no prior knowledge of Ethnozootechny. However, statistically significant differences were observed in perceptions of its importance for inclusion in Course Pedagogical Projects, with greater agreement in the majority group, as well as in the perceived potential contribution of Ethnozootechny to professional training and in interest in research and teaching in the area. The results indicate that, despite limited familiarity with the concept, there is considerable openness toward incorporating Ethnozoo

title: When change meets the classroom: Teachers' acceptance and implementation of new curriculum standards in foreign language education
abstract: Abstract Curriculum reform is a global priority, yet a persistent policy–practice gap remains, which, in very broad terms, shows misalignment between policy intentions and classroom realities. Drawing on a model‐guided systematic review, this article synthesizes 23 peer‐reviewed empirical studies (2015–2024) in foreign language education and propose the Situated Acceptance and Implementation Model (SAIM) as the framework for examining how contextual structures, motivational dispositions and behavioural processes interact in shaping teachers' engagement. Our findings reveal that acceptance depends primarily on curriculum clarity, teachers' beliefs and perceived classroom relevance, whereas sustained implementation hinges on Institutional Governance , Instructional Infrastructure and assessment–curriculum alignment. The analysis also reveals that systemic barriers such as high‐stakes testing, top‐down mandates and ambiguous policy communication limit reform sustainability, while teacher autonomy and collegial collaboration function as critical enablers. title: Assessing interdisciplinary understanding: Disciplinary crossroads in the International Baccalaureate Middle Years Programme
abstract: Abstract Assessing interdisciplinary learning within school curricula remains a persistent challenge in educational research. Difficulties in articulating shared assessment criteria, alongside differing disciplinary and pedagogical perspectives, have contributed to ongoing uncertainty around how interdisciplinary learning should be evaluated. This study explores interdisciplinary assessment in the International Baccalaureate (IB) Middle Years Programme (MYP) where teachers are required to design, implement and assess one interdisciplinary unit involving two or more subjects in each year of the five‐year curriculum. Semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 15 teachers from six MYP international schools in Germany and Switzerland to examine their beliefs and experiences around assessment practices. The data were analysed using thematic analysis and revealed a wide range of perspectives on interdisciplinary assessment. Drawing on Veronica Boix‐Mansilla’s well‐establisehd framework for assessening, interdisciplinary student work, this study focused on three core elements: disciplinary grounding, integrative leverage and critical stance. title: Enacting historical thinking in the history curriculum: Textbook representation and teacher mediation in Turkish secondary education
abstract: Abstract This study examines how historical thinking is translated from curriculum policy into classroom‐oriented curricular practice in Turkish secondary history education. Focusing on ninth‐grade history textbooks published in 2009 and 2018 by the Ministry of National Education and on teachers' perspectives, the study explores how historical thinking skills are represented, interpreted and enacted across different curricular layers. The revised conceptual framework defines historical thinking as a multidimensional form of disciplinary reasoning involving chronology, evidence, contextualisation, perspective taking, interpretation, inquiry and judgement. A qualitative design was employed, combining structured qualitative document analysis of textbooks with a phenomenologically informed teacher‐response strand based on an online semi‐structured interview form completed by 23 history teachers. title: Evaluation of interprofessional collaboration in a teaching session in patient partnership in pharmacy education
abstract: Abstract Patient partnership in health education promotes collaborative and humanistic care. In pharmacy education, however, this approach remains uncommon. We aimed to co‐construct and assess a teaching session on pain management and dispensing refusal, involving patients as full partners. A participatory approach was used. A first focus group (patients, educators, pharmacist, educational researcher, student) defined the curriculum's goals and key skills. A second focus group co‐developed a video of a dispensing refusal scenario. The final session, integrated into the third‐year pharmacy curriculum, used this video and Wooclap® for interaction. Student self‐efficacy and attitudes were assessed via pre/post‐questionnaires and focus group feedback. Interprofessional collaboration was analysed using D'Amour's framework. Students reported better knowledge of pain types and analgesic mechanisms, but also stronger soft skills: listening, non‐judgement, and patient support. They increasingly recognized the importance of explaining treatment and adapting strategies. The co‐construction process strengthened collaboration between team members. title: Procedural justice and writing‐process transparency in GenAI ‐affected writing curriculum: A classroom‐based study of course review governance
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges writing curricula because final texts alone no longer show how student work was produced, revised and justified. This exploratory classroom‐based study examined whether course‐level procedures for handling GenAI‐related writing concerns were associated with students' writing‐process transparency. In an elective academic writing course at a university in China, four intact classes were allocated within instructor strata to procedural governance, emphasising explanation, student response and correctability or techno‐deterrence governance, centred on detector‐threshold warning and routine follow‐up. Students submitted a minimum evidence package comprising outlines, drafts, revision traces and literature‐search records. Procedural governance was associated with higher end‐of‐term writing‐process transparency than techno‐deterrence governance (Hedges' g = 0.48), with the clearest difference in revision traces ( g = 0.50). It was also associated with higher perceived procedural justice ( g = 0.59) and lower false‐accusation anxiety ( g = −0.41). title: Design of an undergraduate course on Storigami for child development
abstract: Abstract This paper is a part of a larger study that discusses and explains the design, implementation and evaluation process of a 14 week face‐to‐face elective course on Storigami for the child development departments. In this study, the design process of the course is explained as the first phase of the project. The creation of the course is based on a student‐centred approach to promote conceptual understanding of the undergraduate students (Hansen, E. J. 2011). Idea‐based learning: A course design process to promote conceptual understanding . Routledge.). The planning and the content of the course are constructed upon the needs of the 21st century higher education and professional life. An integrated course design process and model (Fink, L. D. (2013). Creating significant learning experiences: An integrated approach to designing college courses . John Wiley & Sons.) was employed. There are three phases to this course design process, namely: initial design phase, intermediate design and final design phase. title: Internationalization of the curriculum in teacher education in Türkiye: Evidence from course syllabi at high‐ranking public universities
abstract: Abstract This article examines how internationalization is documented in the formal curriculum of undergraduate teacher education in selected high‐ranking public universities in Türkiye. Drawing on internationalization of the curriculum and internationalization at home, it reports a qualitative document analysis of 20 course syllabi purposively selected from public universities in the Research, QS and THE strata. Using deductive content analysis, the study coded each syllabus against six indicators covering international literature, intercultural or global learning outcomes, global frameworks, language of instruction, mobility or virtual collaboration, and inclusive or multicultural emphasis. The findings indicate that internationalization is present in the documented curriculum, but in limited and uneven ways. Eleven of the 20 syllabi contained at least one indicator, yet most included only a single element. Traces appeared more often in some Content Knowledge and General Culture courses than in Pedagogical Knowledge, while cross‐stratum differences remained modest and descriptive. Empowering teacher‐led stewardship: Going beyond skill acquisition in the age of AI
Thresholds: The metaphorical foundations of powerful knowledge
abstract: Abstract This paper advances a theoretical account of threshold concepts as metaphorical‐relational structures that reorganise meaning across contexts. Building on conceptual metaphor theory, we propose that threshold concepts can be understood as sites of schema‐level reorganisation: deep, embodied patterns of relational logic that scaffold abstract reasoning and enable integration across disciplinary domains. In combination with legitimation code theory, this framing offers one account of why threshold concepts may be experienced as both transformative and troublesome, linking their epistemic role in structuring knowledge with the cognitive challenge of internalising unfamiliar organising logics. We illustrate the framework through the social construction of reality (SCOR) as an integrative threshold concept in the social sciences and humanities. SCOR exemplifies how symbolic boundaries and their historical reconfiguration operate as cognitive and epistemic anchors for understanding phenomena from citizenship to cultural identity. title: Teacher agency under centralised curriculum reform: Divergent sensemaking in Türkiye's Life Studies curriculum
abstract: Abstract This study examines how elementary teachers interpret and enact the Life Studies curriculum within the Century of Türkiye Education Model (CTEM), a large‐scale, centrally steered curriculum reform. Using Q methodology to model shared patterns of subjectivity, 39 teachers sorted 35 statements about curriculum aims, pedagogy, support and implementation conditions. Three distinct viewpoint profiles emerged: (1) Outcome‐Focused Supporters, who strongly endorse CTEM's intended aims while critiquing limited responsiveness to implementation challenges; (2) Process‐Focused Critics, who value participatory, activity‐rich learning but foreground shortages of time, materials and resources; and (3) Implementation Realists, who express relative confidence in system‐level problem‐solving channels while sharply questioning the extent of teacher voice in enactment. Across profiles, teachers converged on the curriculum's pedagogical and civic promise, yet diverged on the conditions that enable or constrain enactment in a centralised system. title: Curriculum in Professional Practice: Curricular justice as professional practice
Reimagining curriculum through the pedagogy of love: A reflection from Indonesian Madrasah
abstract: Abstract Contemporary curriculum debates have increasingly prioritized standards, competencies, and measurable learning outcomes, often overlooking the ethical, relational, and affective dimensions of education. This reflective article reimagines curriculum through the lens of the pedagogy of love, drawing on insights from the Indonesian madrasah context. Rather than proposing a new curriculum model, the article conceptualizes pedagogy of love as an ethical and professional orientation that informs teachers’ curricular judgement and everyday pedagogical practice. By engaging with scholarship on care ethics, relational pedagogy, and curriculum studies, the discussion argues that meaningful curriculum enactment is grounded in relationships characterized by trust, empathy, respect, and compassion. A reflective illustration from a madrasah classroom demonstrates how pedagogical decisions rooted in love can integrate academic learning with students’ emotional, moral, social, and spiritual development. The article further contends that curriculum coherence emerges not only through alignment of objectives, content, and assessment but also through teachers’ moral agency and responsiveness

title: Curriculum alignment with international graduate attribute standards in engineering education: The CPUT experience
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a qualitative case study of how the Mechanical Engineering Diploma programme at Cape Peninsula University of Technology (CPUT) systematically aligned its curriculum with both national and international graduate attribute (GA) standards. The study examines the intentional integration of GAs across all 3 years of the programme in line with the Engineering Council of South Africa (ECSA) framework and the International Engineering Alliance (IEA) accords for engineering education. Drawing on curriculum documents, review feedback and aggregated student performance data, the paper explores how Outcome‐Based Education (OBE) and constructive alignment principles underpin curriculum design, teaching strategies and assessment practices. Key institutional mechanisms, including GA mapping matrices, sub‐minimum assessment policies, and evidence‐based moderation processes, are analysed to show how CPUT ensures that every graduate attains competence in all twelve prescribed attributes. Findings indicate a high level of GA attainment among students, supported by continuous quality improvement cycles informed by stakeholder feedback and external accreditation evaluations

title: Generative AI , virtual reality simulation and communication entrustment in competency‐based medical education
abstract: Abstract Competency‐based medical education (CBME) requires learners to demonstrate communication as observable professional practice rather than theoretical knowledge. Immersive virtual reality (VR) simulation provides authentic opportunities to rehearse challenging clinical conversations, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers new possibilities for communication training. This correspondence argues that AI should function as a bounded reflective scaffold rather than as a substitute for live communicative performance. AI can support preparation and post‐simulation reflection by helping learners explore alternative responses, clarify reasoning and strengthen reflective practice. However, during simulated or assessed encounters, communication should remain entirely learner‐enacted to preserve the validity of entrustment decisions. Positioning AI outside the live interaction maintains professional agency, ensures assessment is based on observable human performance and protects the integrity of competency‐based progression. title: Curriculum integration in policy and practice: Alignment and obstacles for teaching
abstract: Abstract In recent years, curriculum integration has been highlighted in international education policy as a response to global societal issues. Drawing on documents and teacher interviews, this study investigates how curriculum integration is conceptualized in education policy and national curriculum and how this aligns with teachers' understandings and experiences. The study focuses on the most recent national curriculum in Norway, the Knowledge Promotion Reform 2020, which introduced three integrated curriculum topics designed to permeate school practices. The theoretical framework draws on Deng's (2010) domains of curriculum reform and Drake and Burns' (2004) approaches to curriculum integration. Analysis reveals conceptual differences between policy and curriculum. Further, the teachers aim for higher degrees of integration than what is required in the national curriculum. Finally, the study finds that teachers experience several obstacles to integrated teaching, including a lack of formal structures for collaboration across subjects as well as subject‐specific goals and assessment systems.

title: Design and validation of a green curriculum model for technical and vocational education (a mixed‐methods study)
abstract: Abstract Interconnected environmental challenges—ranging from climate change to resource depletion and pollution—have repositioned education from the mere transmission of knowledge towards cultivating the capacity for responsible action. In this context, technical and vocational education and training (TVET), given its close ties to the world of work and technology, stands at the forefront of the transition to a green economy. Yet, in many TVET programmes, sustainability remains confined to broad recommendations or additive content and is not translated into a coherent, assessable curriculum architecture. Accordingly, this study aimed to design and validate a green curriculum model for TVET, elevating sustainability to a guiding criterion for the design and evaluation of curricular elements. An exploratory sequential mixed‐methods design was employed. In the qualitative phase, a research synthesis approach was used to examine scholarly literature, comparative studies and national and international policy and upstream documents. title: Enhancing the professional development of pre‐service English‐language teachers through reflective practice: Implications for curriculum development and practice
abstract: Abstract This study offers guidance for teacher educators and practicum mentors on integrating critical reflection into undergraduate English‐language teacher‐education programmes to strengthen pre‐service teachers' reflective competence, based on insights gained in a study conducted in Kazakhstan. Using a social theoretical lens, it examines professional learning through reflective practice, defines reflective competence and discusses when, how and why reflection is necessary. The article recommends embedding reflective practice into undergraduate English‐language teacher‐education curricula using a structured model that promotes reflection before, during, after and beyond lessons and practical activities to be used with the model to help pre‐service teachers learn to reflect effectively, preparing them for reflective experiences during school‐based teaching internships and future teaching careers. A pre‐implementation qualitative evaluation of the model's pedagogical value, contextual suitability and feasibility is then reported. title: The in/visible curriculum: Noticed, named, enacted
Adapting to the skill‐based curriculum: An examination of teachers' curricular noticing of tools and technology
abstract: Abstract This study investigates middle school mathematics teachers' curricular noticing skills for the integration of tools and technology within the context of a skill‐based curriculum. We focus on the cognitive processes that underlie teachers' curricular noticing of mathematical tools. The data were acquired via semi‐structured interviews and written materials. Through a qualitative exploratory study involving six in‐service teachers, we identified three distinct interpretative and responsive positions: (1) advanced, in which teachers align with the curriculum's intent by employing tools as epistemic instruments for mathematical construction; (2) developing, in which teachers exhibit an inverted workflow– emphasizing the measurement of established rules rather than their development; and (3) limited, in which the dynamic nature of technology is either disregarded or regarded as merely decorative. The findings contribute to the existing literature by emphasizing the inverted workflow as a significant barrier to the implementation of reforms, suggesting that curricular responsiveness is constrained not merely by content knowledge but also by teachers' epistemological understandin

title: A novel Integrated Concept Map–Small Group Discussion ( ICM – SGD ) teaching technique among medical students
abstract: Abstract Concept maps provide an effective visual framework for medical students to organise and integrate complex information, thereby enhancing comprehension and long‐term retention. Similarly, Small Group Discussions (SGDs) promote active learning through interaction, reflection and collaborative problem‐solving. Although both methods are individually effective, there is limited evidence on their combined impact on medical students' performance. To evaluate the association between the Integrated Concept Map–Small Group Discussion (ICM–SGD) technique and academic performance among medical students compared with traditional PowerPoint‐based lectures. This study was conducted at Saveetha Medical College and Hospital , where the ICM–SGD technique was implemented for first‐year (2021 batch) and second‐year (2020 batch) MBBS students. Their academic performance was compared with that of previous cohorts taught using conventional methods. Combined final examination scores across core subjects were analysed using independent‐samples t ‐tests, and Cohen's d effect sizes were calculated to determine the magnitude of improvement. title: Extracurricular activities and equity in Kyrgyzstan: A comparative case study of soviet and post‐independence eras
abstract: Abstract This study examined access to extracurricular activities (ECA) in Kyrgyzstan's primary education during the Soviet and post‐independence eras within the context of equal opportunities, through a comparative instrumental case study based on teachers' perspectives. A qualitative approach was adopted, involving semi‐structured interviews with 28 teachers. Themes were identified via reflexive thematic analysis, resulting in seven main themes: ECA conceptualisation, types of ECA activities, inter‐period comparisons, equity in access, adequacy, funding challenges and problems in ECA implementation. Findings indicate that ECA is viewed as a holistic tool supporting student development, socialisation and moral education; however, post‐independence reductions in state support have exacerbated access inequalities, perpetuating social stratification. In the Soviet era, free, widespread and ideologically oriented ECAs (sports, arts, science) were state‐funded with high infrastructure support (90% participation), whereas today reliance on family contributions, teacher out‐of‐pocket expenses and sponsors (63% urban, 37% rural participation) deepens disparities. title: Profiling teachers' beliefs about learner‐centred teaching in the implementation of Ghana's new K‐9 curriculum
abstract: Abstract Recently, the Government of Ghana introduced the new K‐9 curriculum, known as the Standards‐Based Curriculum, in basic schools, with learner‐centred teaching and learning as its central focus. However, much of the existing research has focused on teachers' self‐efficacy and concerns about curriculum implementation, with relatively limited attention to teachers' beliefs. This study examined teachers' beliefs regarding the use of learner‐centred teaching within the context of the new K‐9 curriculum using the latent profile analysis framework. Data were collected through an online survey in which a standardised questionnaire was administered to 282 basic school teachers from participating schools. The findings identified two distinct belief profiles: one characterised by strong learner‐centred orientation and another characterised by conditional learner‐centred beliefs with concurrent endorsement of teacher‐centred views. Further analysis using logistic regression revealed that years of teaching experience and participation in professional development significantly predict teachers' belief profiles.

title: Epistemic anatomy of the reform‐based secondary chemistry curricula
abstract: Abstract This study examined the epistemic anatomy of the reform‐based 9–12 chemistry curricula in Türkiye, focusing on how learning outcomes embed opportunities for disciplinary epistemic reasoning. Using document‐based qualitative content analysis, 329 learning outcomes were analysed through Epistemic Practice Demands (EPDs), encompassing 47 analytical codes, eight epistemic categories and six hierarchical levels. Findings revealed a procedurally rich but epistemically narrow curriculum. Inquiry formulation, experimental design and comparative reasoning were strongly emphasized, whereas evaluative, justificatory and model‐based practices remained limited. Conceptual engagement dominated the epistemic hierarchy, while interpretive, argumentative and abstract reasoning were peripheral. In comparison with prior Turkish curriculum analyses, these results indicate continuity in curricular orientation, where previously identified cognitive concentration at conceptual and understanding levels corresponds to a deeper epistemic asymmetry privileging procedural over evaluative and theoretical practices. The study further argues that this imbalance reflects not only curricular design but al

title: A comparative analysis of ‘development governance’ and ‘development management’ curricula in selected international universities
abstract: Abstract This study presents a comparative analysis of ‘Development Governance’ and ‘Development Management’ curricula across selected elite international universities. It aims to identify structural patterns, pedagogical approaches, and evaluation strategies to inform curriculum design in developing countries. Utilizing a qualitative methodology based on Berliner's Neo‐formal model, the research analysed 13 postgraduate programmes (Master's and Doctoral) from leading institutions in the Global North. Data were collected from official programme specifications and syllabi. The findings reveal a structural dichotomy: Master's programmes primarily function as professionalizing instruments, emphasizing technocratic skills and project management, whereas Doctoral tracks operate as academic stewardships focused on theoretical abstraction and independent research. The study also identifies a pedagogical tension between the efficiency logic of ‘management’ and the accountability logic of ‘governance’. The results suggest that effective curriculum design in developing contexts may benefit from a hybrid approach that integrates these dimensions while remaining mindful of potential issues of

title: Character education as curriculum‐making in the humanities: A scoping review
abstract: Abstract This scoping review examines how character education is conceptualised and enacted within humanities curricula across international contexts. While character education is widely promoted as supporting the development of ethical, civic and relational dispositions, its place within curriculum design remains contested, particularly in subjects concerned with interpretation, values and human experience. Drawing on the literature spanning curriculum policy, disciplinary pedagogy and moral education, this review synthesises evidence on how character‐related aims are embedded in humanities subjects such as literature, history, philosophy and social studies. Following PRISMA‐ScR guidelines, 806 records were screened, with 26 empirical studies and policy documents analysed in depth. The review identifies two broad patterns of curricular integration: explicit approaches, where virtues or character outcomes are formally articulated in curriculum frameworks and learning objectives, and implicit approaches, where character development is pursued through pedagogical practices, classroom dialogue and interpretive engagement with disciplinary content. title: Curricular justice in an age of compliance: Practitioner dialogues on professional agency
abstract: Abstract This article explores curricular justice in an age of compliance. Drawing on a recorded dialogue among six educators working across elementary, secondary, district and university contexts in Ontario, Canada, we examine how contemporary accountability regimes shape professional agency and curriculum‐making. Organized around three guiding questions—whose knowledge counts, how accountability might be reclaimed and how curricular justice might be reimagined—the dialogue is treated as a methodological site of knowledge production. We argue that curricular justice cannot be achieved through compliance‐oriented policy alone. Instead, it depends on relational, dialogic and professionally grounded practices that current governance structures often constrain. Participants describe how inclusion frameworks may leave inequitable curricular structures untouched, while standardization, surveillance and deprofessionalization narrow educators’ capacity to respond to students and communities. We suggest that this post‐curriculum condition, in which policy discourse eclipses curriculum as lived practice, is also a site of possibility. title: Issue Information
Perceived importance and didactic difficulty of chemistry education: Insights from Czech teachers
abstract: Abstract This empirical study examines how chemistry teachers in lower and upper secondary schools in the Czech Republic evaluate the content of the chemistry curriculum, focussing on its perceived importance and didactic difficulty. Based on a quantitative survey ( N = 146), the study provides insight into the pedagogical content knowledge of experienced teachers. Statistical methods included the chi‐squared goodness‐of‐fit test, the chi‐squared test of independence and multiple correspondence analysis. The results show that topics requiring integration with mathematics and other science subjects are perceived as particularly demanding. They also indicate that teachers consider some part of the chemistry curriculum to be unimportant yet difficult to teach (e.g., particulate structure of matter, chemical reactions and factors influencing their rate, chemistry and society, chemical equilibrium, heat changes during chemical reactions, reaction rate). These findings are discussed in relation to the development and reform of the chemistry curriculum and teacher professional development.

title: The neoliberal metamorphosis of curriculum in Ethiopian higher education: A critical policy analysis
abstract: Abstract This study interrogates the radical restructuring of higher education curriculum in Ethiopia, unmasking the ideological forces that have repositioned the university from a site of critical intellectual socialization to an instrument of technocratic market utility. Guided by the critical theories of Henry Giroux, Michael Apple and Michel Foucault, the research employs a Critical Policy Analysis (CPA) of a longitudinal policy ensemble, including national proclamations, strategic roadmaps and competency frameworks. The study reveals a systematic metamorphosis of the curriculum into a corporate regime. The findings delineate tripartite trajectories: (1) a regulatory shift that employs legal mandates to centralize curricular control; (2) an epistemological shift that displaces theoretical depth with market‐ready competencies, resulting in a systematic de‐theoretization of knowledge; and (3) a structural shift that institutionalizes a 70:30 STEM‐to‐humanities ratio, creating an ‘epistemological apartheid’. title: Reimagining the GCSE English resit curriculum—A dialogue between further education practice and decolonial pedagogy
Conceptualising pedagogical content knowledge for writing through the lens of curriculum statements: A comparative case study
abstract: Abstract This study explores the knowledge required for teaching writing by considering how writing and learning to write are conceptualised in Norway's and Aotearoa New Zealand's curricula. Using Shulman's concept of Pedagogical Content Knowledge as a lens, it examines the explicit and implicit knowledge requirements of the curricula that have implications for teachers' interpretation and implementation work. While previous research focused on the craft of writing, this study adopts a broader perspective, encompassing competencies, context and society. The findings reveal three main categories of knowledge—about (1) language and texts as objects or resources for meaning making, (2) how to act and interact with these resources and (3) purposes of writing at individual and societal levels. The study uses the metaphor of ‘multifocal lenses’ to illustrate teachers' need to operate across multiple planes of focus, from linguistic resources and various subject matters to the roles of writing within the societies' collective cultures and histories.
